# Tutorial: Espresso ontology

## Introduction

In this tutorial, you'll build a small knowledge base about coffee drinks using the okb CLI. It goes one step at a time and ends with an ontology that passes every check. It takes about an hour.

An [ontology](../../../docs/GLOSSARY.md#concept-ontology) is a shared, precise vocabulary for one subject. Say a café wants software that answers "what's the difference between a cortado and a latte?" The software has to know that both are milk drinks, and that one has twice the milk. An ontology is where you write that down so a program can check it. The Learn page [What is an ontology?](../../../docs/learn/ontologies.md) explains the idea in a few minutes.

This tutorial is a sibling of the [wine tutorial](../../wine/tutorial/0-intro.md). It follows the same eight steps. It also covers things wine doesn't: a class with two parents, a fact that sits on a link, and rules that come from a document.

## Who it's for

Developers who are comfortable in a terminal. You don't need to write code or know anything about ontologies. You don't need to know coffee either.

## What you'll build

A small ontology of espresso drinks: the drinks, what goes into them, and a short café menu.

## Before you start

Install okb and check that `okb --help` works. The [Quickstart](../../../docs/getting-started/quickstart.md) shows how.

## Create the ontology

Run the [`okb init`](../../../docs/CLI.md#cmd-init) command to make a folder named `espresso` and call the ontology "Espresso drinks":

```bash
okb init espresso --name "Espresso drinks"
```

```text
✓ Created ontology 'Espresso drinks' in espresso

Step 1 of 8: Determine the domain and scope

  Goal: Write down what the ontology is about, what it's for, who will use and maintain it, and
  which questions it must answer.
  Why it matters: Scope is what lets you say 'no' to things later. Without it, every interesting
  fact looks like it belongs, and the ontology never finishes.

Questions to answer
  • What is the domain that the ontology will cover? (One sentence.)
  • What are we going to use the ontology for? What app, search, report or decision will it
  feed?
  • What types of questions should it be able to answer? (These become competency questions.)
  • Who will use it, and who will maintain it? Do they use the same words for things?
  • What is related but deliberately out of scope?

You're done when
  ○ Domain and purpose are written down
  ○ Users (and ideally maintainers) are named
  ○ At least three competency questions
  ○ At least one thing is explicitly out of scope

Tips
  • Competency questions are a sketch, not a contract. You'll add and change them.
  • Don't try to list every question now. Write a few examples; each stands for a family of
  similar questions, and okb will suggest the rest of the family once a question is answered
  (okb cq link).
  • Good questions are specific and answerable: 'Which wines go with grilled meat?' beats 'Tell
  me about wine'.
  • Include a few questions that need relationships (X goes with Y), not only lookups (what
  color is X).

In the paper's wine example
  Domain: wine and food. Purpose: suggest good wine–food combinations. Out of scope: winery
  inventory, restaurant staff. Questions: 'Is Bordeaux a red or white wine?', 'Does Cabernet
  Sauvignon go well with seafood?', 'What is the best choice of wine for grilled meat?'

Commands
  okb scope   okb cq add

Next: cd espresso && okb scope --domain "..." --purpose "..." --users "..."
```

```bash
cd espresso
```

## Read the output

- okb made a folder with three files: `okb.json`, `nodes.json` and `edges.json`. Every command from here on changes them.
- Each command appears in a block you can copy. What okb printed appears in a separate block under it.

> **Common mistakes**
>
> - **Running commands outside the folder.** okb looks for `okb.json` in the current folder, so run `cd espresso` first.
> - **Editing the files by hand.** Use the commands. They check your work as you go.

## Next step

You made an empty ontology. Next, you'll say what it's for and which questions it must answer.
